title: AI-Assisted Software Development
outcome: Direct AI coding tools to produce software you can defend, and review what they produce for correctness, security and maintainability well enough to own the result.

phases.name: Directing, Not Typing
phases.outcome: Turn a request into a specification precise enough that its output can be judged without you, and triage the first draft in minutes.

modules.name: What Actually Changes
modules.objective: Say precisely which parts of development an AI tool takes over, which it does not, and where accountability stays regardless.
lessons: The job is now specification and review
What a coding tool is actually doing when it "writes" code
Four tasks it does well, four it does badly, and why the split isn't random
Fluent output is not correct output
Where accountability sits when the tool wrote it
practice: Sort twenty real tasks into delegate, direct, or do-it-yourself
lab: Map one week of your own work against what you'd delegate
A one-page delegation map with a stated reason for every call

modules.name: The Executable Spec
modules.objective: Write a specification precise enough that whether its output is right can be settled without asking you.
lessons: Why "make it better" produces nothing you can check
Inputs, outputs, and the cases at the edges
Stating the constraints a tool cannot infer
Acceptance criteria as the first thing you write
Specs that survive being handed to someone else
practice: Rewrite eight vague requests as executable specs
lab: Spec a feature, then have it built from the spec alone
A spec plus the code it produced, every acceptance criterion checked off or explained

modules.name: Context Is the Whole Job
modules.objective: Assemble the context a tool needs to produce code that fits the codebase it has to live in.
lessons: The tool knows nothing about your codebase unless you show it
Choosing what to include: the files that actually constrain the answer
Conventions, house style, and the cost of not stating them
Project instruction files and what belongs in one
When more context makes the output worse
practice: Assemble context for six change requests in an unfamiliar repo
lab: Write the project instruction file for a repo you didn't build
An instruction file plus two changes made with and without it, compared

modules.name: Reading the First Draft
modules.objective: Decide within minutes whether generated output should be refined, rewritten, or thrown away.
lessons: The first ninety seconds: what to look at first
Does it do the thing? Behaviour before style
Invented APIs, plausible names, and functions that don't exist
Silent scope creep: the changes you didn't ask for
The refine-or-restart call, and why restarting is usually cheaper
practice: Triage ten generated diffs against the requests that produced them
lab: Triage a backlog of six generated changes and justify each verdict
A triage table with a refine/rewrite/discard call and a one-line reason per change

modules.name: Knowing When to Take Over
modules.objective: Recognise the situations where directing a tool costs more than writing the code yourself.
lessons: The prompt loop: three attempts and no closer
Problems whose hard part is the thinking, not the typing
Unfamiliar domains: when you can't review what you asked for
Small precise edits, where manual is simply faster
practice: Call take-over or continue on eight stalled sessions
lab: Instrument a week and log every take-over and what it cost
A decision log and a revised personal take-over rule with evidence behind it

phases.name: Reading Code You Didn't Write
phases.outcome: Read an unfamiliar diff for intent, control flow, data shape and dependency cost fast enough to review it properly.

modules.name: Reading for Intent
modules.objective: Reconstruct what a piece of code is trying to do before judging whether it does it.
lessons: Read the signature, then the return, then the middle
Naming as evidence — and as misdirection
Comments that describe code that no longer exists
Reconstructing the requirement from the implementation
Saying what a function does in one sentence
practice: Summarise eight unfamiliar functions in one sentence each
lab: Reverse-engineer the spec of a module nobody documented
A written spec of existing behaviour, with every assumption you couldn't verify listed

modules.name: Control Flow and State
modules.objective: Trace every path through a piece of code, including the ones nobody thought about.
lessons: Tracing a happy path by hand
Every branch is a promise about a case that exists
Early returns, guard clauses, and the paths they hide
Mutable state and who else can change it
Loops that terminate, and loops that only usually terminate
practice: Enumerate the untested paths in seven functions
lab: Path-map a generated function and find the case it forgot
A path table with inputs, expected results, and the gap you found

modules.name: Data Shapes and Boundaries
modules.objective: Find the places where the shape of data crossing a boundary is assumed rather than checked.
lessons: What the function believes about its input
Null, empty, missing and zero are four different things
Boundaries: where validation actually has to happen
Types that lie, and types that only describe the happy case
Serialisation, encoding, and the data that changes shape in transit
practice: Find the unchecked assumption in eight boundary crossings
lab: Harden the boundary of a generated API handler
A validated handler plus the list of inputs that used to get through

modules.name: Dependencies and What They Cost
modules.objective: Judge whether a dependency an AI tool reached for should be in your project at all.
lessons: Why tools add libraries you didn't ask for
Reading a package before you install it
Licences, and the ones that follow your code out the door
Packages that don't exist: hallucinated imports and the squatters waiting for them
The maintenance you inherit with every import
practice: Accept or reject seven dependencies with a written reason
lab: Audit the dependency additions in a generated pull request
A dependency review with a keep/replace/remove call and evidence per package

modules.name: Tests as a Reading Tool
modules.objective: Use a test suite to learn what code is supposed to do — and notice when the suite is lying.
lessons: Tests as the only executable documentation you have
Reading a test to find the requirement behind it
Tests that pass because they assert nothing
Mocks that make the test agree with the code, whatever the code does
Coverage as a map of what nobody checked
practice: Spot the tautological assertion in eight generated tests
lab: Review a generated test suite for tests that cannot fail
A review naming every vacuous test with the assertion that should replace it

phases.name: Correctness, Security and Failure Modes
phases.outcome: Catch the specific defects AI tools produce most, before they reach a branch anyone else depends on.

modules.name: The Bugs AI Writes Most
modules.objective: Recognise the recurring defect patterns in generated code and know why the training data produces them.
lessons: Off-by-one, inclusive bounds, and the fencepost that never dies
Copy-paste symmetry errors the eye slides over
Plausible defaults that are wrong for your system
The happy path implemented perfectly and nothing else
Why these patterns recur: what the model learned from
practice: Find the defect in ten generated snippets, one pattern each
lab: Build your own defect-pattern checklist from real output
A checklist of at least eight patterns, each with a real example you caught

modules.name: Injection and Untrusted Input
modules.objective: Find every place untrusted input reaches an interpreter, and close it the way that actually closes it.
lessons: SQL injection: the bug generated database code writes by default
Parameterisation, and why escaping is not the same fix
Command injection and the shell you didn't mean to invoke
Cross-site scripting: output encoding at the right boundary
Prompt injection: untrusted text reaching a model with tools
practice: Trace untrusted input to an interpreter in eight snippets
lab: Close every injection path in a generated CRUD service
A patched service with a written note per fix explaining why it closes the hole

modules.name: Auth, Secrets and Permissions
modules.objective: Check that generated code enforces who may do what, and that nothing secret is where it shouldn't be.
lessons: Authentication and authorisation are different questions
The endpoint that checks you're logged in and nothing else
Secrets in source, in logs, in error messages, in the client bundle
Object-level permission checks and the ID you can just change
Tokens, expiry, and what a stolen one still buys
practice: Find the missing authorisation check in seven handlers
lab: Permission-audit a generated multi-user feature
An audit listing every endpoint, the check it makes, and the check it should make

modules.name: Concurrency, Time and Ordering
modules.objective: Find the assumptions about ordering and simultaneity that generated code makes without saying so.
lessons: Two requests at once: the read-then-write that loses data
Idempotency, retries, and the payment charged twice
Time zones, clock skew, and dates that are off by a day
Async code that awaits nothing, and errors that vanish
Transactions: what is actually atomic here
practice: Name the race condition in eight concurrent scenarios
lab: Make a generated booking flow safe under simultaneous use
A corrected flow plus the interleaving that broke the original

modules.name: Error Handling and Failure Paths
modules.objective: Judge whether code fails in a way anyone can diagnose, or fails silently and expensively.
lessons: The catch block that swallows the error and returns null
What the caller can actually do about this failure
Partial failure: the half-finished write nobody rolls back
Error messages written for the person who'll be paged at 3am
Timeouts, retries and backoff that don't make things worse
practice: Rewrite eight error paths so failure is diagnosable
lab: Rebuild the failure handling of a generated integration
A revised integration with a failure table: what breaks, what the user sees, what the log says

phases.name: Agentic Workflows
phases.outcome: Run multi-step AI work — decomposition, tool access, verification of a chain rather than a completion — without losing control of the blast radius.

modules.name: Decomposition and Task Design
modules.objective: Break work into steps an agent can complete and you can verify one at a time.
lessons: Why one big task fails and six small ones don't
A step is done when something checkable is true
Ordering steps so a failure stops cheaply
Steps that need a human between them
Writing the plan before anything runs
practice: Decompose seven feature requests into verifiable steps
lab: Plan a multi-file change as a step chain with checkpoints
A written plan with a verification condition for every step

modules.name: Tools, Files and Blast Radius
modules.objective: Decide what an agent may touch, and make the worst case survivable.
lessons: What the agent can reach is what it can break
Read, write, execute, network: granting the minimum
Working on a branch, a copy, or a container
Destructive operations that need a human hand on them
Recovering from an agent that did the wrong thing thoroughly
practice: Set the permission boundary for eight agent tasks
lab: Configure a sandboxed workspace for an autonomous change
A working sandbox config plus a written worst-case recovery plan

modules.name: Verifying a Chain, Not a Completion
modules.objective: Check that every step of a multi-step run actually did what it claimed.
lessons: "Done" is a claim, not a result
Reading a run log for what was skipped
The step that silently failed and the four built on top of it
Independent verification: checking the artefact, not the transcript
Cheap checks you can run after every step
practice: Audit eight run logs for unverified claims
lab: Verify an agent run end to end against its own plan
A verification report marking every step done, partial, or not done, with evidence

modules.name: Long Tasks, Context and Handoff
modules.objective: Keep long-running work coherent across context limits, restarts and days off.
lessons: What gets lost when the context window fills
Writing state down so a restart isn't a reset
Handing a task back to yourself two weeks later
Summaries that keep the decisions and drop the noise
Knowing when to start clean instead of continuing
practice: Write the handoff note for seven interrupted tasks
lab: Run one task across three sessions with no loss of thread
A task file whose state let a cold restart continue without re-deciding anything

modules.name: When Agents Go Wrong
modules.objective: Recognise the characteristic failure modes of autonomous runs early enough to stop them.
lessons: The confident loop: repeating a failing approach
Goal drift: solving a nearby, easier problem
Deleting the test instead of fixing the code
Fabricated verification: claiming a check that never ran
Stop conditions you set before you start
practice: Name the failure mode in eight transcripts
lab: Write a post-mortem of a run that went wrong
A post-mortem naming the failure mode, the earliest visible signal, and the stop condition that would have caught it

phases.name: Shipping and Operating
phases.outcome: Get AI-assisted changes through tests, review, CI and deploy — and be able to operate what you shipped.

modules.name: Tests You Can Trust
modules.objective: Write and commission tests that would actually fail if the code were wrong.
lessons: A test is a claim about behaviour someone will rely on
Specifying tests instead of asking for "some tests"
The cases a generated suite always misses
Mutation thinking: would this test notice?
Fast, deterministic, and independent — or nobody runs them
practice: Strengthen eight weak tests so they can fail
lab: Commission and harden a suite for an untested module
A suite where every test has been shown to fail against a deliberately broken version

modules.name: Review Workflow and PR Craft
modules.objective: Put an AI-assisted change in front of another human in a form they can review.
lessons: The pull request description as the reviewer's only context
Splitting a large generated change into reviewable pieces
Disclosing what was generated, and why it matters to the reviewer
Responding to review on code you didn't write
Reviewing someone else's AI-assisted pull request
practice: Rewrite seven pull request descriptions for a cold reviewer
lab: Split and describe a 900-line generated change
A stack of reviewable pull requests, each independently mergeable and described

modules.name: CI, Builds and Reproducibility
modules.objective: Make the build fail on your machine before it fails on someone else's.
lessons: It works here: the environment you forgot you had
Lockfiles, pinned versions, and reproducible installs
Reading a CI failure that didn't happen locally
Flaky tests and the trust they cost
Gates worth having: what must pass before merge
practice: Diagnose eight CI failures from logs alone
lab: Make a generated project build the same way twice
A project that builds clean from a fresh checkout, with the differences you removed listed

modules.name: Deploy, Rollback and Migrations
modules.objective: Ship a change you can undo, including the ones that touch stored data.
lessons: The question before every deploy: how do I undo this
Schema migrations that are safe to run while it's live
The generated migration that drops a column someone reads
Feature flags: shipping code without shipping behaviour
Backwards compatibility across a rolling deploy
practice: Judge the rollback story of eight proposed deploys
lab: Turn a destructive generated migration into a safe sequence
A staged migration plan, each stage independently reversible

modules.name: Observability and On-Call Reality
modules.objective: Instrument a change so that when it misbehaves in production you can find out why.
lessons: The log line you'll wish you had written
Structured logs, and what belongs in one
Metrics that tell you something is wrong before a user does
Alerts that are worth waking someone for
Debugging generated code you last read a month ago
practice: Instrument seven code paths for a 3am diagnosis
lab: Instrument a generated service and diagnose a seeded fault
A diagnosis traced to the fault using only the logs and metrics you added

phases.name: Working as an AI-Assisted Developer
phases.outcome: Scope, price, disclose and defend AI-assisted work — and prove it on one change you take from request to shipped.

modules.name: Estimating and Scoping
modules.objective: Estimate AI-assisted work honestly, including the review time that is now the bulk of it.
lessons: Why generation speed doesn't shorten the job
The unknowns that make an estimate a guess, said out loud
Renegotiating when the estimate was wrong
practice: Estimate seven briefs and state what would break each one
lab: Estimate a real brief and track the variance
An estimate, the actual, and a written account of where the difference came from

modules.name: Accountability, Licensing and Disclosure
modules.objective: Know what you owe a client or employer about how the code was produced, and what you carry if it's wrong.
lessons: You shipped it, so it's yours
What generated code may carry with it
Client policies, NDAs, and what you may paste into a tool
Disclosure that is honest without being theatre
When to refuse work you can't review
practice: Decide the disclosure obligation in seven situations
lab: Write your own AI-use policy for client work
A one-page policy you would send a client before starting

modules.name: Working With a Team, and Without One
modules.objective: Collaborate on AI-assisted code asynchronously, on your own hours, without becoming a bottleneck.
lessons: Async by default: writing so nobody has to ask
Getting review when you're the only one who understands it
Disagreeing about generated code without relitigating the tool
Being the person who can't take a call today
Building a review habit when there's no reviewer
practice: Rewrite seven synchronous asks as async ones
lab: Run a full change through async-only collaboration
A change record where every decision is written down and nothing needed a meeting

modules.name: Cost, Limits and Tool Independence
modules.objective: Work with a clear picture of what your tools cost, where they fail, and what happens when they're gone.
lessons: What a working day of tool use actually costs
Rate limits, outages, and the deadline that doesn't move
Keeping the skill you'd need without the tool
Local and offline options, honestly compared
practice: Cost and de-risk seven tool-dependent workflows
lab: Deliver a change with your primary tool unavailable
The finished change plus a note on what slowed down and by how much

modules.name: Capstone — Ship and Defend a Change
modules.objective: Take one real change from request to shipped, and defend every decision in it.
lessons: The brief, and what it doesn't say
Planning the change against your own take-over rule
Reviewing your own work as a stranger would
Writing the defence: why this, not that
What you'd do differently with another week
practice: Rehearse the defence against seven reviewer challenges
lab: Ship the capstone change and defend it in writing
A merged change, its tests, its disclosure note, and a written defence of every significant decision
